h1:
Tha Sadet Market
Mekong Riverside Lao-Vietnamese Souvenirs
intro: Tha Sadet Market is an old market on the Mekong that has been part of Nong Khai for generations. Older locals still call it the Indochina Market because the goods come from Laos, Vietnam and China all mixed together down one strip. One walk gets you woven cloth, silk, mu yo (Vietnamese pork sausage), Lao coffee, shiitake mushrooms and all sorts of dried goods — plus a view across the river to Vientiane and the Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge. This guide tells you straight where each thing sells, what's actually worth taking home, and how to haggle so you walk away with the good stuff.

blocks.html: If you come to Nong Khai and skip Tha Sadet Market, you haven't really seen the place. The market runs in a long line along the Mekong inside the municipal area, right next to the riverside road and the Naga Park promenade where people like to stroll. What sets it apart is the mix of Lao, Vietnamese and Chinese goods — Nong Khai is a border town that has traded with Vientiane for ages, and it has a sizable Thai-Vietnamese community, so the souvenirs and dried goods here are the real thing, not just stuff cranked out for tourists.

The market is almost entirely roofed, so it's an easy walk even in strong sun or rain. The path is one long lane running parallel to the river, with fairly clear sections for food, dried goods, cloth and household items. Walking end to end at a relaxed pace takes about 1–2 hours.

blocks.text: What zones are inside the market

blocks.html: Before you dive in, knowing the rough layout helps you find what you want faster. Tha Sadet Market breaks down loosely into a few zones, each strongest in something different.

items.name: Food & riverside zone
items.blurb: Near the entrance and along the water — pâté, naem nueang (fresh spring rolls), khao piak sen (rice noodle soup), Vietnamese coffee and stalls with river views. A good spot to start with a meal or coffee before you shop.

items.name: Dried goods & souvenirs zone
items.blurb: Mid-market — mu yo, Chinese sausage, prunes, dried lukyee, shiitake mushrooms, Lao coffee and imported processed foods. This is where most people stock up to take home.

items.name: Cloth & clothing zone
items.blurb: Handwoven cloth, silk, pha khao ma (checked cotton), sarongs and local-style clothing, plus cheap clothes from the Lao and Chinese side. Haggling welcome.

items.name: Household & odds-and-ends zone
items.blurb: Kitchenware, kai krata egg pans, bags, shoes, watches, small appliances, toys and a wide range of cheap Chinese goods.

blocks.title: How to walk it smart
blocks.html: Start at the riverside food zone and fuel up first, then head deeper into the dried-goods and cloth sections once you're full — you'll choose better than shopping hungry with bags already in hand. Eat the fresh stuff on the spot; save the dried goods and cloth for the end, right before you leave.

blocks.text: Dried souvenirs actually worth taking home

blocks.html: The beauty of Tha Sadet Market is how easily you can take dried goods home — no worrying about them spoiling, fine for hauling onto a bus or plane, and many shops will vacuum-seal them for you. Here's what people buy and what you'll find better here than at an ordinary market, because it comes straight from Laos, Vietnam and China.

items: Mu yo, Chinese sausage & Isan sausage — Nong Khai's number-one souvenir. The Vietnamese-style mu yo is springy and keeps for days; ask the shop to vacuum-seal it and you can carry it onto a flight.
Lao / Vietnamese coffee beans — dark-roasted and bold. Buy a bag along with a Vietnamese phin filter and brew it yourself at home.
Prunes, lukyee & dried fruit — imported processed snacks, all in the middle zone. Sold by the kilo, and many shops let you taste before you buy.
Dried shiitake & Chinese herbs — for the home cooks, cheaper here than in the big cities.
Rice paper (krayo) — take it home to wrap your own naem nueang or spring rolls. Keeps a long time and weighs almost nothing.
Kai krata egg pans & Vietnamese kitchenware — the small dimpled pan for Nong Khai-style skillet eggs. A souvenir for the cooks in your life, and only a few places stock it.

blocks.text: Woven cloth, silk & pha khao ma — how to choose without getting burned

blocks.html: Tha Sadet Market is a riverside cloth source people come specifically to browse. There's everything from handwoven Isan-pattern cloth, silk, pha khao ma and sarongs to local-style clothing and fabric from the Lao side. Prices range widely, from a few hundred to a few thousand baht depending on the fabric and how much of it is handwork.

items: Pha khao ma — the easiest cloth souvenir to buy: a few hundred baht a piece, endlessly useful, and a popular grab-and-go gift.

Handwoven Isan-pattern cloth & sarongs — mat mi (ikat) and local patterns. Check the fabric and how even the pattern is before buying; handwoven patterns won't be as perfectly uniform as printed ones.
Silk — both pure silk and blends, with big price gaps. If you want pure silk, ask the shop straight and feel the fabric across a few shops before you decide.
Ready-made clothes & Lao fabric — cheap clothing from the Lao and Chinese side, good for casual travel wear. Don't expect fine detailing.

blocks.title: Read the cloth like a pro
blocks.html: Handwoven and machine-printed cloth differ in price by several times over. Handwoven patterns won't track perfectly straight and you'll see the silk threads joining; printed cloth looks unrealistically smooth and even. If you're serious about pure silk, feel and compare across 2–3 shops and ask prices straight before you commit. Don't rush the first stall.

blocks.text: Strolling the Mekong around the market

blocks.html: Tha Sadet Market isn't just shopping. Around it are Nong Khai's riverside landmarks, all walkable in the same trip if you want more atmosphere than retail.

items: Naga Park on the river — the naga statue and riverfront walkway next to the market, a photo spot and a place to catch the cool breeze in the evening.
Vientiane view & Friendship Bridge — across the river you'll see the Lao side, with the first Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge not far off.
Wat Lamduan / old-town temples — easy to carry on from the market and pay your respects in the old-town district.
Riverside cafés — if the market wears you out, there are cafés right by the water to sit, rest and take in the view before heading back.

blocks.text: How to time your Tha Sadet Market walk

blocks.html: The market is open all day, so timing is flexible. Below is a rhythm that works well — adjust it whether you arrive in the morning or the afternoon.

items.activity: Enter from the riverside, breathe in the morning air, take in the Lao-side view and photograph Naga Park.
items.note: Few people this early — easy walking.

items.activity: Light breakfast — khao piak sen or hot pâté with a Vietnamese coffee.
Hit the dried-goods zone — pick out mu yo, Chinese sausage, Lao coffee, shiitake and prunes.
items.note: Taste before you buy; ask for vacuum-sealing if you're flying.

items.activity: On to the cloth zone — browse pha khao ma, woven cloth and silk, comparing prices across 2–3 shops.
items.note: Haggling welcome; don't rush the first stall.

blocks.label: Afternoon–evening
blocks.title: Grab household bits, then enjoy the view

items.activity: Walk the household zone — kitchenware, kai krata egg pans and odds and ends from China.
items.note: The souvenirs for home cooks are in this zone.

items.activity: Finish with a riverside coffee and a view of the Friendship Bridge.
items.note: The market closes at 18:30 — no need to rush.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Most shops take cash, so bring plenty of small bills. Haggling is normal, especially for dried goods and cloth, but sit-down restaurants usually have fixed prices. Some items are labelled as coming from Laos or Vietnam but are really Chinese — judge by quality rather than trusting the sign. Weekday late mornings are quiet and easy to walk; weekends and holidays have more shops open but bigger crowds.

faq.q: What time does Tha Sadet Market open?
faq.a: It's open daily from roughly 07:00 to 18:30. The market is roofed, so you can walk it in strong sun or rain. Fresh food is out from early morning, while the dried-goods and cloth zones can be browsed all day. A weekday late morning is the most comfortable time — fewer crowds than on weekends.

faq.q: Are Tha Sadet Market and the Indochina Market the same place?
faq.a: Yes, they're the same. People call it the Indochina Market because the goods come from Laos, Vietnam and China all mixed together. It sits on the Mekong inside Nong Khai's municipal area, next to Naga Park, with a view of the Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge from the riverside.

faq.q: Which souvenirs are worth taking home from Tha Sadet Market?
faq.a: Mu yo, Chinese sausage and Isan sausage top the list — ask the shop to vacuum-seal them and you can carry them onto a flight. Beyond that, there are Lao and Vietnamese coffee beans with phin filters, prunes, lukyee, dried shiitake, rice paper for wrapping naem nueang, and the Vietnamese-style kai krata egg pan.

faq.q: Is the woven cloth and silk here real, and roughly how much does it cost?
faq.a: There's handwoven cloth, pure silk, silk blends and printed cloth, with prices ranging from a few hundred to a few thousand baht. Pha khao ma at a few hundred baht a piece is the easiest souvenir to buy. For pure silk, ask the shop straight, feel and compare the fabric across several shops, and yes — you can haggle.

faq.q: Does Tha Sadet Market take cards, and can you bargain?
faq.a: Most shops take cash, so bring enough small bills. Haggling is normal, especially for dried goods, souvenirs and cloth, while sit-down restaurants usually have fixed prices.
